subtype: Approach: leaving work to the last month [Pitfall]
passage: Farida, you asked how our project went wrong, so here it is, from me, Mahima. We decided early it was easy: a small app, a small database. "We'll do it in a weekend," someone said, and everyone laughed. So September went by with lunches and cricket. In late October we finally sat down to code. Each of us had written a part, and none of the parts fit. One person's dates were text and another's were numbers, the login broke the reports, and there were four days before submission. We stayed up two nights and got it to work, barely. The viva went badly because we could not explain half the choices. We were confident, and that was the problem.

qa.q: When did the team finally sit down to code?
qa.a: They finally sat down to code in late October.

qa.q: What is Mahima feeling as the project story ends?
qa.a: Mahima feels regret and embarrassment about the rushed submission and the poor viva, adding that being confident was the problem.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team have used, and why?
qa.a: They could have set small early milestones with dates, because that exposes integration bugs while there is still time to fix them.

qa.q: How might Farida see Mahima's account?
qa.a: Farida, who asked what went wrong, hears an honest story with no excuses, so Farida may feel able to ask about the details too.

grounding: Shows a team assuming the project is easy and delaying the coding until late, then facing integration bugs and a barely working submission.

subtype: Approach: leaving work to the last month [Pitfall]
passage: I live two doors down from Pranav in the hostel, so I saw his project year from the corridor. In August, he and Alka told everyone their inventory app was easy. "Two weeks of coding, max." September and October were cricket and fest season. In November they said, "After the mid-terms." In the first week of March, a month before submission, I started hearing keyboards at 2 am. Alka came over most nights with her laptop. The login module worked on Pranav's machine and crashed on hers. The database didn't talk to the app. One night I heard Pranav say, "Nothing fits together." They submitted on the last day, with a video instead of a live demo, because the live version kept freezing. I don't know how they felt about it. They didn't talk about the project for weeks after.

qa.q: When did the late-night coding begin?
qa.a: In the first week of March, a month before submission.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling when he said nothing fits together?
qa.a: Pranav was probably panicked and exhausted, realising the parts they had assumed were easy would not join up.

qa.q: What else could the pair have done in August?
qa.a: They could have built a small working version early and joined the parts from the start, so joining problems showed up in time.

qa.q: How is Alka affected by the late start?
qa.a: Alka ends up coding most nights and dealing with crashes on her own laptop, sharing the stress of the rushed finish.

grounding: Shows a team sure the project is easy putting off coding until the last month, then hitting integration bugs and submitting a barely working version.

subtype: Approach: leaving work to the last month [Pitfall]
passage:
August. Kunal and Sunaina read their project brief, a campus lost-and-found app, and laughed. "We can build this in two weekends." They told their guide they'd start after the fest.
March. With four weeks left, they finally opened the code editor. The upload page worked alone. The search page worked alone. Together, they crashed. Sunaina's database design didn't match what Kunal's screens expected. They stayed in the lab until the guard switched off the lights, three nights in a row. Kunal's eyes were red; Sunaina stopped answering her family's calls.
April. On submission day, their app ran only if nobody searched with a space in the words. In the viva, the external examiner typed "blue bottle". The screen froze. Kunal stared at the floor. Sunaina said quietly, "We started too late, sir." The examiner nodded and wrote something down.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when the screen froze?
qa.a: Kunal felt ashamed and defeated, staring at the floor.

qa.q: What would you change first about their plan?
qa.a: Start in August with a small version that connects the upload and search pages early, so mismatches show up months before the viva.

qa.q: How might the external examiner see the project?
qa.a: The examiner sees a fragile app and an honest admission, likely judging that the idea was fine but the planning was not.

grounding: Illustrates a team that thought the project easy leaving coding to the final month, then facing integration bugs and a barely working submission.
